solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: City beset by division, creating fear (5)

indicators.note: to be beset is to be surrounded on all sides, so the city ends up inside

blocks.note: an arm is a division or branch of an organisation

annotation.surface: A city torn apart by internal division, and the population frightened by it.
annotation.walkthrough: Here 'division' is a branch, as in an arm of the armed services, not a split between factions.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: alarm is the sudden fright felt at danger.

entries.clue: Bishop in Costa Rica clumsily tumbling (10)

indicators.note: letters handled clumsily get dropped and picked up out of order

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A bishop on a visit to Costa Rica loses his footing and goes sprawling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clumsily tumbling' reads as one phrase about the bishop falling; the split puts 'clumsily' with the wordplay and leaves 'tumbling' as the definition. The B joins the fodder, which is why 'in' is there.
annotation.definitionFit: Tumbling in the gymnastic sense, somersaults and handsprings, is one branch of acrobatics.

entries.clue: Intend to acquire weapons after change of heart (3)

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter, and here that letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: to arm is to acquire weapons

annotation.surface: Someone planning to arm themselves after a change of mind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Intend to acquire' looks like the definition phrase, but 'to acquire weapons' is all wordplay, the verb. The clue does not say which letter replaces the heart; the definition decides it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: you aim to do what you intend to do.

entries.clue: Mary Quant creation worn by flunkey (6)

blocks.note: Mary Quant popularised the miniskirt in 1960s London
a garment being worn is on

annotation.surface: A footman dressed up in a miniskirt from the Swinging Sixties.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Worn by' looks like an instruction to dress the flunkey; it is just a two-letter word placed after the skirt.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are servile hangers-on who do a superior's bidding.

entries.clue: Challenge half-cut Tory going after comic (5,2,2)

indicators.note: read literally, cut in half: only two of TORY's four letters remain
going after means following, so TO is placed behind the comic

annotation.surface: A tipsy Conservative politician following a comedian's act.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which is the surface; in the wordplay it means cut in half. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to stand up to someone is to confront and resist them, so challenge them.

entries.clue: The latest worry about work permit’s introduction (4,5)

indicators.note: about means around, so the worry surrounds the other letters
a word's introduction is where it begins, its first letter

annotation.surface: Anxiety over the start of a new work-permit scheme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The latest' looks like it wants the newest worry; it is the definition. Stop press was late news squeezed into a newspaper after printing had begun.
annotation.definitionFit: Stop press is the newspaper column for the very latest news, added once the presses were rolling.

entries.clue: Product trials? Moving head of analytics helps (5)

indicators.note: moving a letter changes its place in the word; here the head of analytics, A, shifts

blocks.note: beta tests, trial versions of a product
A, the first letter of analytics, moves from the end to the front

annotation.surface: A company asks whether moving its analytics chief will help its product testing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head of analytics' reads as a job title; it is a single letter already in the word, which is shifted to the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually with a shady edge: to abet is to help, especially in wrongdoing.

entries.clue: Claimed Conservative and Liberal are for the most part bound by act (8)

indicators.note: most of ARE, not all of it: the last letter goes
the letters are tied up inside the act, as a prisoner is bound

annotation.surface: Two political parties are said to be mostly tied by an act of parliament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Act' suggests an Act of Parliament to go with the parties; it is simply a deed, which holds the other letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to declare something is to state it as true, to claim it.

entries.clue: Agent upset, cutting off patient (11)

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, and in a down clue a word knocked over reads upward, reversed

blocks.note: a rep is a sales agent, reversed

annotation.surface: An agent annoyed at being cut off while dealing with a hospital patient.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like a noun, a person in hospital; it is the adjective, and 'cutting off' looks like being cut off on the phone.
annotation.definitionFit: Near synonyms as adjectives: someone persevering keeps going steadily, which takes patience.

entries.clue: Defer to old Turkish governor (4)

blocks.note: a bey was a governor in the Ottoman Empire

annotation.surface: Bowing to the authority of a former Ottoman official.
annotation.walkthrough: BEY is a crossword regular, worth knowing along with DEY and AGA.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: deferring to someone means yielding to their wishes, doing as told.

entries.clue: Feature Abramovich is familiar with, they say (5,4)

indicators.note: what people say is what is heard, so the letters come from the sound

blocks.note: Roman Abramovich, the Russian businessman; knows = is familiar with

annotation.surface: Something the billionaire and former Chelsea owner happens to be acquainted with.
annotation.walkthrough: Abramovich is there only for his first name. Roman Abramovich owned Chelsea football club from 2003 to 2022.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a nose with a high, prominent bridge is one kind of facial feature.

entries.clue: Nothing removed from curriculum? Damn (5)

indicators.note: something removed from a word is taken out of it, here the O

blocks.note: a course of study is a curriculum

annotation.surface: A student exclaims in frustration at a syllabus with nothing left in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Curriculum? Damn' reads as a student's groan; the question mark splits the wordplay off from the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to damn someone is to call down a curse on them.

entries.clue: Foolishly forbid entry for migrant (4,2,7)

indicators.note: the letters are arranged foolishly, not in their sensible order

blocks.note: a passage is an entry or way in

annotation.surface: A complaint that it is foolish to refuse entry to a migrant.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is an immigration argument; the answer is a bird that migrates. Only 'forbid' is jumbled; 'entry' is taken as it stands.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a bird that migrates, and figuratively a person who drifts from place to place.

entries.clue: Ingenious clue for “sure”? Possibly (11)

indicators.note: the letters could possibly be something else if rearranged

annotation.surface: A setter wonders whether a clever clue for the word 'sure' is possible.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'sure' look like the answer being clued; they just mark it as a word, and all three words are fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a resourceful person finds clever, ingenious ways round problems.

entries.clue: Rocket Man’s writer on the radio (10)

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard, not seen, so the spelling may differ

blocks.note: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island

annotation.surface: Elton John's song Rocket Man and its lyricist, heard on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rocket Man' points at Elton John, whose lyrics Bernie Taupin wrote; here it is George Stephenson, whose locomotive Rocket won the 1829 Rainhill trials.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic label: George Stephenson built the steam locomotive Rocket, so he is the man behind it.

entries.clue: Soviet assets putting the squeeze on news agency (4)

indicators.note: the two words squeeze the answer tightly between them

annotation.surface: Soviet state resources being used to pressure a news organisation.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer belongs in the scene: TASS was the Soviet state news agency.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: TASS is the Russian, formerly Soviet, state news agency.

entries.clue: Conclusion of Hamlet perhaps (10)

blocks.note: the resolving of a dispute or a deal
a hamlet is a small village, one example of a place where people live

annotation.surface: How Shakespeare's Hamlet ends.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital H makes Hamlet the prince; it is a small village, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a settlement.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the conclusion of a dispute, and a place where people have settled, of which a hamlet is one kind.

entries.clue: Abandoned streets capturing island’s melancholy mood (9)

indicators.note: done with abandon, without restraint, so the letters run wild
the rearranged streets capture and hold the island's letters

blocks.note: STREETS rearranged, to be split around the island's letters
the S of the apostrophe-s comes along too

annotation.surface: Deserted streets on an island creating a gloomy atmosphere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' paints empty streets; here it means wild. The word is French for sadness.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French: tristesse is sadness, a melancholy state of mind.

entries.clue: Criticised when society grew weak (8)

annotation.surface: Someone attacked at a time when society was in decline.
annotation.walkthrough: 'When' looks like part of the story's timing; it is the small word 'as', a common swap.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: to assail is to attack, and verbal attack is criticism.

entries.clue: Liner owned by its hands, reportedly (6,4)

indicators.note: a report is heard, so the letters come from the sound

blocks.note: the hands are the crew, so a ship owned by them is the crew's

annotation.surface: A liner run as a cooperative, owned by the sailors who work it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are sailors, the crew of a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an ocean liner carries passengers, and today most such ships sail for pleasure.

entries.clue: Feeble colonel losing head (4)

indicators.note: a word's head is its first letter, and losing it drops the B

blocks.note: Colonel Blimp, the pompous reactionary of David Low's British cartoons

annotation.surface: A weak army officer who has lost his nerve, or been decapitated.
annotation.walkthrough: Colonel Blimp was a British cartoon character of the 1930s; a blimp is now any pompous, reactionary type.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something limp lacks firmness or vigour, as a feeble handshake does.

entries.clue: Dealer quietly accompanying court official (6)

indicators.note: to accompany is to go alongside, so the P goes right next to the court official

blocks.note: an usher keeps order in a law court

annotation.surface: A drug dealer slipping quietly into court beside an official.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface already has the dealer in court; 'Dealer' is the drug seller, not a card dealer or trader.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense: a pusher is someone who sells illegal drugs, a dealer.

entries.clue: Students don’t easily understand Marxist concept (5,8)

blocks.note: a class is a group of students
to struggle is to find it hard

annotation.surface: Students finding Marx's ideas hard to grasp.
annotation.walkthrough: The pun: the class struggles with class struggle.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: class struggle, conflict between economic classes, is central to Marxist theory.

entries.clue: Young lover in Washington possessed by lust? (5)

indicators.note: something possessed is held, so Washington is held inside the sin

blocks.note: lust is one of the seven deadly sins
WA is the postal abbreviation of Washington state

annotation.surface: A young man in the US capital overcome by desire.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags lust as just one example of a sin.
annotation.definitionFit: An old poetic word: a swain is a country youth, and by extension a young suitor.

entries.clue: Bit of a bother following two females around America (4)

indicators.note: the two females stand around America, one on each side

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references

annotation.surface: Some trouble involving two women touring the United States.
annotation.walkthrough: The F for 'following' goes last, though the clue puts that word first: it follows the rest. Faff is British slang for fuss or bother.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal: a faff is a time-wasting fuss, a bit of bother.

entries.clue: Terrible, just abandoning pound (5)

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so the pound's letter is left out of the word

annotation.surface: A shameful decision to drop the pound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'merely'; it is the adjective, fair or lawful.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: awful and terrible both mean very bad.

entries.clue: Dramatist unfortunately clashes with you, just outside (9)

indicators.note: things going unfortunately are in disarray, and so are the letters
just the outside letters of YOU are used

annotation.surface: A playwright regrets falling out with you, just as you stand outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Just outside' reads as a place; it means 'only the outside' of the word before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Aeschylus, author of the Oresteia, was the earliest of the great Greek tragic dramatists.

entries.clue: Piloted precursor to Zeppelin? (3)

blocks.note: to pilot is to guide or steer
the word that comes before Zeppelin in a famous rock band's name

annotation.surface: An airship flown before the Zeppelin was invented.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Precursor' suggests an earlier airship; it is the word that comes before Zeppelin in the name of the rock band Led Zeppelin.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: piloted means guided, the past of lead, and Led is the first word of the band's name.

entries.clue: Traditional steps to take? (4,5)

blocks.note: belonging to the customs of ordinary people, handed down
the surface wants a course of action; the setter means footwork

annotation.surface: Asking what the customary procedure is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Steps to take' reads as a course of action; the steps are literal footwork, and traditional ones make up a folk dance.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: a folk dance is a sequence of traditional footwork, literally steps you take.

entries.clue: Creator of works barely crumbling away (5)

indicators.note: stripped bare: the outer letters are removed

blocks.note: the first and last letters go

annotation.surface: Artworks that are only just falling apart.
annotation.walkthrough: Auguste Rodin was the French sculptor of The Thinker. 'Barely' looks like 'hardly'; here it strips the word bare.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Rodin created sculptural works such as The Thinker and The Kiss.
